steps.say: Liver injuries are graded from small surface cracks to complete shattering. Small capsular tears behave very differently from deep splits through major vessels, and the grade points toward watching or operating.
steps.tx: **AAST** (trauma organ injury scale) grades liver injury **I to VI** (one to six) from **subcapsular haematoma** (blood under the capsule) under **10 percent** (ten percent) surface to hepatic avulsion, with **grade III** (grade three) over **3 cm** (three centimetre) depth marking major injury.

steps.say: A stable patient with a sore belly but no guarding and steady pulse can heal without an operation. Rest, repeated blood counts and follow-up scans carry the great majority through safely.
steps.tx: **Haemodynamically stable** (steady pulse and pressure) blunt injury without peritonitis suits **nonoperative management** (watchful care without surgery) with bed rest, serial haemoglobin and follow-up scanning, succeeding in over **85 percent** (eighty five percent) of cases across modern trauma centres with intensive monitoring.

steps.say: A bright blush of contrast on the scan means active bleeding at that moment. Stable patients can still be watched closely, but a dropping pressure with a blush sends the patient to the radiology suite for blocking the vessel.
steps.tx: **Contrast blush** (active dye leak on scan) with instability goes to **angioembolisation** (radiology vessel blocking), while a blush in a stable patient without peritonitis can be watched with rescanning and transfusion thresholds in a high-dependency setting with immediate surgical backup available.

steps.say: When bleeding will not stop and the patient is cold, acidotic and coagulopathic, the surgeon packs the liver tightly, closes temporarily and leaves the rest for another day. The packs come out once physiology recovers.
steps.tx: Major bleeding in **damage control** (abbreviated life-saving surgery) gets **perihepatic packing** (pads compressing the liver) with laparotomy pads, with relook and pack removal at **24 to 48 hours** (one to two days) after correcting cold, acid and clotting in intensive care with blood products.

vis.alt: Open abdomen showing packed liver, stapled bowel loops and a temporary closure dressing.
vis.caption: Damage control laparotomy: perihepatic packing around a lacerated liver with stapled bowel and temporary closure. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Tears reaching the great veins behind the liver bleed faster than anything else. Standard clamping fails here, so the surgeon must isolate the whole venous segment or shunt blood past the injury.
steps.tx: **Juxtahepatic venous injury** (tears of veins behind the liver) with retrohepatic caval bleeding needs **atriocaval shunt** (tube bypassing the segment) or **total vascular exclusion** (clamping all inflow and outflow), carrying mortality over **50 percent** (fifty percent) even in expert hands with full vascular control.

steps.say: Days after the accident the patient vomits dark blood and passes black stools with aching under the right ribs. Blood has found a channel into the bile ducts. The same dye test that finds it can block it.
steps.tx: Delayed **haemobilia** (blood in the bile) with melena and right upper pain days after trauma comes from an **arteriobiliary fistula** (artery-to-duct connection), diagnosed and treated by hepatic angiography with embolisation of the culprit branch in one sitting without open surgery.

vis.alt: Anatomy diagram showing an artery-to-duct connection with clotted blood inside the bile channel.
vis.caption: Haemobilia: arteriobiliary fistula with intraductal clot bleeding through the ampulla. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Bile leaking into the belly forms a pocket that can be drained through the skin, while lowering pressure inside the ducts lets small leaks seal on their own. A completely severed duct needs a new join to bowel.
steps.tx: Bile leak and **biloma** (walled bile pocket) after trauma get endoscopic **sphincterotomy** (duct mouth cut) with stenting to lower ductal pressure, while major ductal disruption needs hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction to bowel by an experienced biliary surgeon at a specialist hepatobiliary centre.

steps.say: Knife and bullet wounds that pierce the belly wall need opening without delay, especially with bowel contents spilling out. Inside, laying the wound track open and tying single vessels beats removing whole lobes.
steps.tx: **Penetrating injury** (stab or gunshot through the wall) with peritonitis or evisceration goes straight to laparotomy, and **tractotomy** (laying the wound track open) with selective vessel ligation beats formal lobectomy for through-and-through wounds, preserving maximum functioning liver for recovery afterwards.
